Honors educators have the responsibility to eliminate underdeveloped honors contracts that dilute rather than enrich the academic experiences of students. (Wyatt, 195.) It is good practice for evaluation and assessment templates to be created and provided by the honors organiza- tion.
And oversight of contracts by honors administrators must therefore be well-struc- tured, mandated, and clear, and guidelines must be provided to faculty on deadlines and assessment rubrics.
It is essential that contracted work not simply be “more”; rather, it must be meaningful- ly integrated in each case with the course content and learning goals and the work the course already requires. (Bahls, 177) The contract must therefore measurably outline work that leads to the “broader, deeper, and more complex learning-centered and learn- er-directed experiences” with which the NCHC defines honors education (NCHC).

The suggestion that the learning experience of a contracted class is equivalent to a stand-alone honors class—seeing as the student receives academic credit for both— opens honors programs and colleges up to potential exploitation by administrators who may not see the need for assigning appropriate resources to honors or may even try to cut budgets. (Badenhausen, 11) It must therefore be agreed—and practiced—that when options are limited, contracts are a workable path to honors completion that benefits both the students and the institution, not a work-around for the program or institution to avoid curriculum development and creating classes.
But even though the close community of students and faculty that defines honors edu- cation is achieved here by other means, the importance of achieving a sense of belong- ing to the larger cohort should not be ignored.
Therefore, a stricture should be in place that students be limited in the number of credits they can complete through contracts, especially in their freshman and sophomore years.

Finally, with increasing demands and tightening budgets overburdening faculty with unpaid work that is not recognized in reviews, it is essential that faculty be recognized and compensated for the additional work a contract entails.
Otherwise, faculty fatigue may set in and departments and colleges may resent the outside burdens (Bambina, 118).
The equivalent of a one-credit independent study would seem reasonable, and perhaps an amendment to faculty contracts might state the value of this work for pro- motion and tenure reviews.
Contracts bring honors students into non-honors classrooms, mitigating the separation of honors stu- dents from others.
Contracts are a beneficial part of the honors methods in individual cases, not a substitute for the program.
Students should be a part of an honors cohort, con- tacts should not be allowed to separate them from the group.
Administration must take care to never let contracts become routine or a “secret fix.” Honors admin. must work diligently to maintain high standards, and clear expec- tations Contract-work must mea- surably achieve NCHC goals: broader, deeper, and more complex learning experiences.
Faculty must be rewarded for the work they do, lest fatigue or resentment under- mine the contract system. 5

Presentation of the Fritz Wenisch Award for Exceptional Contribution to the Faculty Senate - President Williams announced that this year’s winner is Furong Xu (College of Education), who served as this year’s Curriculum and Standards Committee (CASC) Chair. Xu’s smooth and skillful handling of the process, during which her good humor and collegiality never waned.

2. Presentation of the Sheila Black Grubman Faculty Outstanding Service Award - President Williams presented the award to Douglass Reed (Arts and Sciences, Philosophy), who served as Administrator Evaluation Coordinator (AEC) for the past two years. Williams highlighted Dr. Reed’s spirit of ‘calm industriousness’ that he brought to the AEC role and noted that he received praise from his colleagues for his diplomacy, tact, and resourcefulness. Williams further noted that before being appointed as AEC, Dr. Reed had served in the Faculty Senate on the Teaching, Advising and Assessment Committee (TAAC) and had brought the same ambitious and proactive energy to that role. 1. Announcement of Election Results - See item 3c above.

i. Bill No. 2025-2026-08A, Courses, covering course modifications in five colleges, and new courses in the Colleges of Business, Pharmacy and Arts and Sciences.
ii. Bill No. 2025-2026-08B, Programs, covering multiple programs in several colleges.
The following proposal was tabled:
iii. Bill No. 2025-2026-08C, covering the new BS in Interdisciplinary Artificial Intelligence proposed by the College of Business. An objection was raised by a Senator from the Department of Computer Science and Statistics, who asserted that their department had not been given an opportunity to comment on possible overlap. A second question was raised about the extent to which ethics will be addressed by the new program and it was suggested that ethical use of AI should be integrated. CASC Chair Xu noted that her committee has a duty to address overlap, but typically, by the time a proposal reaches CASC, overlap should have been addressed or resolved at the level of the department and college curriculum committees. In the subject case, appropriate documentation from the affected colleges was included.

c. General Education Committee - Acting Chair Stark was on hand to field questions about the report. The following was advanced by the Committee, seconded from the floor, and approved.
i. Bill No. 2025-2026-07A, Courses, covering course modifications in three colleges, and three new courses in the College of Arts and Sciences.
d. Curricular Reports from the Graduate Council to the Faculty Senate - Chair Hans Saint-Eloi Cadely was on hand to field questions about the reports. The following were advanced by the Committee, seconded from the floor, and approved.
i. Bill 2025-2026-07A, Courses, covering several course changes across multiple colleges, and new courses in the Colleges of Arts and Sciences, Engineering, and the Environment and Life Sciences.
ii. Bill 2025-2026-07B, Programs, covering and new specialization in the College of Business and a new online certificate in the College of the Environment and Life Sciences.

Committee member Julia Lovett presented the report, thanking her fellow committee members and highlighting their key accomplishments. In addition to reviewing three existing centers for renewal and authorizing creation of a new Institute, the Committee also worked to revise their forms in light of recent legislation, provided feedback on proposed University Manual language in Chapter 8, Section 90, and continued their tracking and oversight functions per their charge, among other things. A motion to accept the report was made, seconded and approved.

f. Research and Creative Activities Committee (CRCA) and SubCommittee Reports – Chair D’Agata thanked the members of her committee and reviewed the committee’s charge. Highlights of AY 25-26 activities included providing support to faculty during an era of rapid change in the research environment. The Committee had also prioritized supporting graduate students who faced unique and exacerbating housing and other financial challenges this year. The Committee has outlined proposed changes to its scope, structure, and strategic alignment with institutional governance over research functions which they hope to formalize during AY 26-27. Subcommittee Chair Wei also thanked fellow committee members, as well as the volunteer reviewers who assisted in reading and ranking applications for Career Enhancement, Proposal Development, and Collaborative Research Development grants. In looking ahead to next year, the Committee noted a need for more reviewers if the number of applications exceeds expectations again. They also noted a need for more explicit guidance to be provided to both proposers and reviewers, which would help to streamline and improve consistency across submissions and evaluations. General Education Committee (GEC) Report - GEC Acting Chair Stark explained that the Committee was focused on assessing the C2 (Global Responsibilities) and D1 (Integrate and Apply) outcomes this year. The results seemed stronger for the D1 outcome than the C2, as students more often approach competency in the D1 areas. Students assessed for C2 outcomes consistently struggle with communicating in a language other than English, considering multiple perspectives, and examining global responsibilities. Questions from the floor centered around C2 findings and whether they represent a structural weakness in foreign language proficiency within the current GenEd framework. Equity, diversity, and inclusion are fundamental values of the American Library Association and are one of ALA’s committed key action areas which act as guiding principles for investment of energies and resources.
ALA’s Office for Diversity, Literacy and Outreach Services also encourages using a social-justice framework of diverse perspectives within LIS to advocate for equitable access to library services for all people.
In an increasingly diversifying country, library and information professionals are in need of critical thinking skills, cultural competency approaches, and new social justice approaches to executing equitable information spaces.
Currently, LIS programs, professional organizations, and LIS-based companies are competitively offering trainings around Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship approaches to LIS.
For example, the New England Library Association (NELA) held a one-day diversity summit in the summer of 2017 with full enrollment, heavily focused on discussing race, racism, gender, sexuality, ability, immigrant and migrant rights, and social justice applications to diverse groups.

The University of North Carolina’s School of Information and Library Science offers a Diversity Advocate Certificate, the LIS press “Library Juice Press Academy” offers a course titled “Exploring and Applying Critical Theory: An Introduction for Librarians,”, and Library Journal has a number of diversity based professional development workshops such as “Diversity and Cultural Competency Training: Collections & RA,” to name a few.
This graduate track is a highly manageable 12-credit program from an accredited institution of higher education.
The proposed track in Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship approaches will prepare LIS graduates for diverse workplaces, serving and collaborating with diverse populations, and recruiting a more diverse workforce, as well as creating equitable information institutes.
This proposed track will be the only such track in New England and as a track, it will also serve librarians across the United States.

Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship supports URI’s mission by supporting diverse communities.

The Department of Criminology and Criminal Justice offers a Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degree.
The interdisciplinary degree in Criminology and Criminal Justice provides students with a wide range of course options so that students may tailor their learning to their educational and professional interests.
Our purpose is to empower our graduates to meaningfully consider, contribute to, and reimagine discourses and decisions about crime and justice.
The CCJ Department does this by making intentional choices about our work and remaining committed to continual professional growth and community building.
The program requires 30-49 credits in the major including CCJ/SOC 230(H) (with a grade of C or better), CCJ/PSC 274(H) (with a grade of C or better), and one of three capstone classes: CCJ 403, CCJ 410 or CCJ/PSC 476.
Students must select one research methods course from the following: ECN 306, PSC 310, PSY 200, or SOC 301.

Students are required to take six elective courses selected from the following two areas: criminology electives – AAF 230; CCJ 200 (approved topics), 334, 370, 400 (approved topics), 403, 410, 450, 476; AAF/HIS 366; PHL 318; PSY 254, 466; SOC 420; criminal justice electives – AAF 230; CCJ 200 (approved topics), 280, 285, 290,,, 332, 333, 381 (must be taken in combination with CHM 391 and/or ITR 305 for a total of 3 credits to count as 1 elective class), 456, 480, 490, 400 (approved topics), 403, 410, 476; CHM 391 (must either be repeated 3 times or taken in combination with CCJ 381 and/or ITR 305 for a total of 3 credits to count as 1 elective class); CCJ/HIS 361, AAF/HIS 366; ITR 305 (must be taken in combination with CHM 391 and/or CCJ 381 for a total of 3 credits to count as 1 elective class) PSC 334, 371, 388, 472; PSY 465; SOC 303.
At least two courses must be taken from each elective area and no more than four courses can be taken in either area.
All electives must be a minimum of 3 credits.
While CCJ 403, 410, and CCJ/PSC 476 are each capstone classes and electives, students may not use the same course to count as both a capstone and an elective class.

When appropriate, and by permission of the Department Chair, students may substitute internship credit (SOC 477, PSC 375/376, PSY 305, or GWS 300) or independent study credit (CCJ 485, SOC 498/499, PSC 455/456, PSY 489, or GWS 450) for one of their elective courses listed above.
No more than 3 credits may be used toward the major from internship or independent study.
Internal transfers into the CCJ major form a different major, or students wishing to add the CCJ major to their current major, must have a minimum 2.50 GPA.
A total of 120 credits is required for graduation.
At least 30 of these credits must be in courses at the 300-level or above.
In order to transfer into the criminology and criminal justice B.A. program from University College for Academic Success, a student must have completed at least 24 credits and have an earned a minimum of a 2.0 GPA.
